result.summary: Creon forbids burial of the Argive dead until Theseus and the Athenians force Thebes to give them up. The Epigoni then sack Thebes under Alcmaeon, who kills his mother Eriphyle, is driven mad, and is finally murdered over the necklace and robe, after which his sons avenge him.

scenes.title: Creon forbids burial of the dead
scenes.summary: Creon leaves the Argive dead unburied and Antigone is entombed alive for burying Polynices. Adrastus appeals to Athens, Theseus takes Thebes, and Evadne dies on Capaneus' pyre.
scenes.stakes: Antigone risks death for burying her brother; Adrastus seeks rites for the fallen.

scenes.title: The Epigoni take Thebes
scenes.summary: The sons of the fallen march under Alcmaeon, defeat the Thebans, and the Thebans flee on Tiresias' advice. Tiresias dies at Tilphussa and the exiles found Hestiaea.
scenes.stakes: Thebes faces destruction; the Epigoni seek vengeance for their fathers.

scenes.title: Spoils sent to Delphi
scenes.summary: The Argives raze the walls and send part of the booty and Manto to Apollo at Delphi.

scenes.title: Alcmaeon's madness and death
scenes.summary: Alcmaeon kills Eriphyle, is pursued by a Fury, marries Arsinoe and later Callirrhoe, and is killed by Phegeus' sons over the necklace and robe.
scenes.stakes: Alcmaeon seeks release from madness but loses his life.

scenes.title: The sons avenge Alcmaeon
scenes.summary: Callirrhoe's sons grow up at once, kill Phegeus' family, dedicate the necklace and robe at Delphi, and colonize Acarnania.
scenes.stakes: The sons risk death in avenging their father.

scenes.title: Euripides' version
scenes.summary: Euripides says Alcmaeon had children by Manto and gave them to Creon of Corinth; Tisiphone was sold, then recovered. Amphilochus founded Amphilochian Argos.
scenes.stakes: Tisiphone is enslaved unknowingly by her own father.

notable_quotes.reason: Antigone's burial of Polynices and punishment, the famous story later dramatized by Sophocles.

analysis.text: Burial rites, vengeance and the cursed necklace drive a cycle of kin-killing across generations.
Apollodorus gathers competing versions, citing Euripides, showing how Greek myth varied between poets and local traditions.

legacy.text: The Antigone story of defying a ban on burial became central to Sophocles' tragedy and later debates about law and conscience.

fun_facts.text: The 'Epigoni' (Greek for 'those born after') gave their name to later imitators or inferior successors.

language_notes.text: The altar of Mercy (Eleos) in Athens was a traditional place of refuge for suppliants seeking help.
The suppliant's bough was an olive branch wrapped in wool, laid on an altar to signal a plea for protection.
Epigoni means "those born afterwards"; the name is given to the sons of the Seven who attacked Thebes.
The robe is the one Polynices gave Eriphyle, as the necklace had earlier bribed her to send Amphiaraus to war; here Thersander bribes her again.
"Loath" means unwilling; Alcmaeon wanted first to punish his mother, as his father had instructed.
Tiresias advises sending a herald to negotiate as a pretext, giving the Thebans time to flee while the enemy waited.
The Fury is an avenging spirit sent to punish kin-murder; her pursuit is expressed as Alcmaeon's madness.
The necklace and robe are the gifts of Harmonia, which Polynices used to bribe Eriphyle to send Amphiaraus to war.
"Stand another trial" means undergo further judgment or purification; the barren land shows the pollution of his matricide had not been cleansed.
"Hied" is archaic for hurried or went quickly.
"Comeliness" means beauty; "begat" is archaic for fathered.

context_notes.text: Creon, brother of Jocasta, became king after Eteocles and Polynices killed each other in the war of the Seven against Thebes.
Theseus was the legendary king of Athens, who here acts as protector of suppliants and defender of burial customs.
Laodamas, son of Eteocles, led Thebes because his father had died in the earlier war.
Tiresias was the blind Theban seer; his death at the spring Tilphussa ends his long prophetic career.
Manto, Tiresias' daughter, was a prophetess; she was offered to Apollo as the finest spoil, to serve his oracle.
Zeus's courting of Callirrhoe is the divine favor that grants her request for her sons' sudden growth.
Amphilochian Argos lay in northwest Greece, near Acarnania, and was named after its founder.

literary_notes.text: Antigone is punished with burial alive for giving burial to her brother, so the penalty mocks her act of piety.
Evadne's leap onto the pyre shows extreme wifely devotion in one brief, stark action.
Tiresias's death at the spring marks the end of Thebes' old order, anticipating the city's abandonment.
The Fury of the murder acts as a pursuing figure, giving guilt and madness a vengeful, almost physical presence.
Phegeus gives the treasures in good faith, and Alcmaeon is killed for them by his own host's sons.
The sons' instant growth is a miraculous exaggeration, stressing how urgent and fated the vengeance is.
